newsitem.title: NORWAY: Amnesty in first meeting with Chinese delegation.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty in first meeting with Chinese delegation.

text.p: Amnesty International, one of the most stern critics of China's human rights record, met a Chinese delegation for the first time on Friday in what it described as a breakthrough in its efforts to expand contacts with the Chinese.

The meeting was arranged at short notice by Norwegian junior foreign minister Jan Egeland at the end of a week-long visit to Norway by an eight-member delegation of the Chinese Society for Human Rights.
The Society is a non-government organisation but Egeland noted it was led by Zhu Mutzli, a former minister of culture and education, and included a Beijing Foreign Ministry adviser.

"It has been a problem that China did not want to speak to the world's biggest human rights organisation," Egeland told reporters after the meeting. "Norway suggested this meeting and the Chinese accepted it."
Nicholas Howen, director of the international wing of the London-based watchdog, said he had a "friendly and honest" meeting with Zhu.
"This was a breakthrough in discussions with civil society in China," he said. "This was a new reaching out. We had previously only spoken to Chinese academics.
"Our ultimate aim must be to contribute to a change in China. Our understanding is that dialoque will lead to pressure for change," Howen said.
Zhu stressed that his group was a non-government organisation, but did not rule out that dialoque with Amnesty could have an impact on Beijing's political leaders.
"But I am not in a position to say what conclusions the Chinese government will draw from this dialoque," he told a separate news conference.
He said the morning-long meeting with Howen and other Amnesty officials showed that "the sides have fundamentally different views on human rights".

"We can't narrow the gap with one single meeting, but I think this was a start. What is important is that we have this dialogue. Our position is that we want a dialogue as long as it is based on equality and mutual respect," Zhu said.
He declined to elaborate on the discussions, but Howen said they touched upon international law, China's use of the death penalty and other issues.

In its latest criticism of Beijing on June 3, Amnesty called on China to take the chance afforded by the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping to reconsider its 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy protests.
Zhu and Howen said they planned to meet again, possibly in Hong Kong, which reverts from British to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
